extracted.intended_audience: experimental scientists, natural philosophers, and informed scientific readers (late-19th-century audience; experimental physicists/chemists and instrument designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing, conducting, recording, and interpreting controlled physical experiments (radiation/cooling apparatus example) and for general practice in scientific discovery and research organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery by careful experiment, observation, and study
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The general method by which [Cronstedt] discovered it was careful experiment, observation, and study of the properties of matter.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated across examples (nickel, phosphorus, Volta, Oersted, Faraday): discoveries arise from careful, sustained experimentation and observation rather than accident. Examples given: Cronstedt isolating nickel; Brandt obtaining phosphorus by distilling urine residue and charcoal; Volta discovering the battery; Faraday discovering magneto-electricity from a minute effect. Anti-pattern: assuming discoveries are generally accidental or ‘fortunate ideas.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter to new and definite conditions to reveal new results
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘by putting matter and its forces under new conditions, observing and studying the results’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit recommendation to change experimental conditions to reveal previously unseen phenomena; many modern trades (telegraph wire manufacturing, electro-plating, etc.) originated from putting matter under new conditions. Use controlled variation of conditions as a discovery strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer systematic, reliable, and abstract investigation over directing research solely to immediate practical results
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Discoveries in science are best made, not by trying to obtain some valuable commercial or technical result (that object belongs to an inventor), but by making new, reliable, and systematic investigations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue research driven by 'love of truth' and abstract inquiry; attempting to force research directly into practical channels can diminish its importance and spirit of inquiry. Historical support: Davy, Hofmann, and coal-tar dye discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour between discovery, invention, and practical manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘there should be a more judicious division of labour, one man to discover new truths, another to put them into the form of practical inventions, and the practical business man to work them’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that faculties for discovery, invention, and manufacture are rarely united in one person; organise teams/roles accordingly to optimise innovation and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support original scientific research with institutional/state provision (laboratory infrastructure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that German practice erecting great laboratories at State expense and making special provision for original scientific research is different from English practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that state- or institution-backed laboratories with dedicated provision improve capacity for original research; implies a standard for funding & infrastructure for systematic investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus design to ensure uniform internal temperature and whole-mass measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a spherical enclosure with a central radiator sustained by tubes, an external annular water-jacket with circulation nozzles, and internal paddle-wheel to produce continuous current from centre to circumference so the central thermometer indicates the temperature of the entire mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features described in detail (sphere 5 in. diameter, radiator 2.75 in., tubes to admit thermometer bulb and axle for paddle wheel, external nozzles for circulating cold water). Rationale: rapid interchange of fluid particles prevents temperature gradients and ensures the central thermometer reflects the whole mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermometer placement and mechanical stirring to improve response and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The upper tube is large enough to admit the bulb of a thermometer, ... the bulb of the thermometer may be inserted considerably beyond the centre of the sphere.’ Rotary motion of the water round the bulb renders its indication prompt and reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the bulb centrally (or beyond centre as specified) and ensure active circulation so indicator responds quickly and uniformly. Use magnifying glass for readings to improve precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and control external/environmental temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The enclosure being maintained at a constant temperature of 33 [°]. A wooden cistern containing 16 gallons, charged with water and crushed ice, is connected by flexible tubes to the nozzles ... a pump being applied ... by means of which the cold water is forced through the apparatus and then returned to the cistern.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control surrounding medium temperature with circulating cold water and ice bath; document the maintained external temperature as part of the method; stable external conditions are necessary to interpret cooling rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple operators with divided, repeatable roles to reduce experimental error
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the investigation has been conducted with the utmost care, four operators having invariably been employed ... Ist operator regulates the temperature... 2nd operator works the pump ... 3rd operator turns the paddle-wheel, and reads the thermometer ... 4th operator ... records the time called.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide tasks (environment control, pump operation, mechanical stirring and reading, and timekeeping) to reduce operator workload, increase consistency, and allow reproducible procedure. This reduces single-operator variability and helps auditing of measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardised timing/reading protocol and use of chronograph; compute mean times to correct irregular readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Readings called when the top of the mercurial column is covered by half the thickness of the line on the scale; times recorded by a Casella chronograph; recorded times irregular so computations are based on mean time which is then used to determine true increment (seconds per 1°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a precise, repeatable reading criterion; use mechanical timing devices to record calls; when observed times are irregular because of human reaction or instrument imperfections, compute mean times and use corrected values for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record observed and corrected data, present tables and diagrams, and compare curves to test theoretical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of a table with observed time, corrected time, and computed increment; diagram with ordinates for observed and corrected times used to show agreement and test Newton’s law (rate of cooling proportional to excess temperature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full tabulated data and plotted curves for both raw and corrected values to visualise deviations; use these to test proportionalities (e.g., Newton’s law) and to detect intersections or systematic biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate and rule out experimental artefacts (e.g., heating from stirring)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It might be supposed that the motion of the water within the radiating sphere... will occasion an elevation of temperature ... Experiments have been made ... but no elevation of temperature has been observed. The diameter of the wheel ... maximum speed ... velocity too small to generate appreciable heat.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test potential artefacts empirically (vary stirrer speed, measure any self-heating) and report negative or positive findings; compute particle speeds and consider whether they are sufficient to introduce heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for temperature-dependent emissive power; do not conflate emissive-power changes with mere temperature changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding that emissive power per degree increases with temperature (e.g., at 65° emissive power 0.0080 unit/°; at 1,800° 0.186 unit/°; at 3,000° 0.337 unit/°). Warn not to confuse increase of emissive power with mere augmentation of temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report quantitative emissive-power values at different differential temperatures; acknowledge that molecular changes alter radiant properties and that this affects interpretations of laws like Newton’s. Be cautious when extrapolating low-temperature laws to high-temperature regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute and discuss sources of discrepancy and measurement uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrepancies (observed vs calculated times irregular) are attributed to difficulty in visual judgement of the thermometer column, imperfect graduation of thermometer, differences in emissive power at different temperatures, and plotting/engraver errors in figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and discuss observer limitations, instrument calibration limits, and plotting/representation mistakes; explicitly state likely causes of systematic or random discrepancies and how they were mitigated (e.g., averaging) or remain as uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in reporting: include procedural detail, numerical tables, and candid notes on minor errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed description of apparatus dimensions, operator responsibilities, pumping and circulation arrangements, measurement protocol, full tables of readings, and editorial note correcting a plotting mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient detail (dimensions, speeds, procedures) to allow replication; include full data tables and point out even small errors in figures or calculations so expert readers can detect and understand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of fundamental research for long-term practical results
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Scientific discovery is the most valuable in its ultimate practical results when it is pursued from a love of truth as the ruling motive ... The greatest practical realities of this age had their origin ... in a search after important new truths, entirely irrespective of what utilities they might lead to.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification for funding/support: emphasise that undirected, curiosity-driven research produces profound practical benefits over time; avoid short-term utilitarian pressure that may reduce the scope of significant discovery.
